hook: In a room of just 23 people, there's a better than even chance two of them share a birthday.
writeup: This is called the Birthday Paradox. It trips people up because we instinctively think about whether someone shares our birthday — a 1-in-365 shot. But the question is whether any pair matches, and with 23 people there are 253 possible pairs. Each pair has a small chance of matching, but those small chances compound: P(at least one match) = 1 − (364/365 × 363/365 × … × 343/365) ≈ 50.7%. By 70 people the probability exceeds 99.9%. This same math is why hash collisions and UUID duplicates happen sooner than you'd expect.

hook: In most real-world datasets, the number 1 appears as the leading digit about 30% of the time — not 11% like you'd expect.
writeup: Benford's Law says that in many naturally occurring datasets — population counts, stock prices, street addresses, river lengths — the leading digit follows a logarithmic distribution. The digit 1 appears first ~30.1% of the time, while 9 shows up only ~4.6%. The intuition: to go from 1xx to 2xx you need to grow by 100%, but going from 9xx to 10xx only requires ~11% growth. So numbers spend more 'time' with smaller leading digits. Forensic accountants use this to detect fraud — fabricated numbers almost never follow Benford's distribution.

hook: The length of a coastline depends on the length of your ruler — and it approaches infinity as the ruler gets smaller.
writeup: The Coastline Paradox shows that coastlines are fractals: the more finely you measure, the longer they get, because every inlet and rock reveals more detail at smaller scales. Measure Britain's coast with a 100km ruler and you get ~2,800km. Use a 50km ruler and it jumps to ~3,400km. Mandelbrot used this observation to develop fractal geometry, arguing that many natural shapes — clouds, mountains, blood vessels — share this property of self-similar roughness at every scale.
